title: Polymorphism (virtual dispatch)
hook: When you call a method through a base-type variable, the Common Language Runtime (CLR) can route the call to the correct derived implementation. That runtime routing is polymorphism — and it only works when you use virtual and override correctly.

blocks.text: **Polymorphism** means "many shapes." In C#, it usually means **subtype polymorphism**: calling `handler.Parse(raw)` through a `AuthHandler` variable invokes the `Parse` implementation of the actual runtime type (`LtiHandler` or `OidcHandler`). The CLR uses a **method table** (also called a virtual dispatch table) to find the right implementation at run time.

entries.plainDefinition: Marks a method or property as overridable. The CLR reserves a slot in the method table for runtime dispatch.
Replaces a virtual or abstract member in a derived type. Participates in runtime dispatch.
A virtual member with no body. The derived type must provide an override.
Declares a new member that hides a base member. Does NOT participate in virtual dispatch — a common interview trap.

blocks.text: Polymorphism lets you write code against a base type and plug in different behaviors. A grading pipeline can accept `AuthHandler` and work with any sealed provider without knowing which one it got. But every `virtual` member is a **compatibility promise** — once shipped, changing or removing it can break derived types. Keep virtual surfaces small, document them, and prefer `sealed override` to close the slot when no further derivation is planned.

blocks.title: override versus new
blocks.body: `override` replaces the slot — calling through the base type hits the derived method. `new` hides the name — calling through the base type still hits the base method. Interviewers love this distinction.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Base declares virtual
items.body: `public virtual string Name => "base";` opens a dispatch slot in the method table.

items.title: Derived declares override
items.body: `public override string Name => "lti";` fills that slot for `LtiHandler`.

items.title: Call through base reference
items.body: `AuthHandler h = new LtiHandler(); h.Name` — the CLR looks up the slot on the runtime type (`LtiHandler`), not the compile-time type (`AuthHandler`).

items.title: sealed override closes the slot
items.body: `public sealed override string Name => "lti";` prevents any further derived type from overriding `Name` again.

diagram.title: Virtual dispatch versus member hiding
diagram.source:
flowchart LR
  CALL["h.Name where h is AuthHandler"] --> CHECK{Is Name virtual?}
  CHECK -->|override| SLOT[Runtime type slot\nLtiHandler.Name = lti]
  CHECK -->|new hiding| BASE[Compile-time type\nHandler.Kind = handler]

snippet.label: override versus new — the interview classic
snippet.explanation: Line 2: `Name` is virtual — opens a slot. Line 3: `Kind` is non-virtual. Line 8: `override` replaces the `Name` slot. Line 9: `new` creates a separate `Kind` member. Lines 12–13: through a `Handler` reference, `Name` dispatches to `LtiHandler` but `Kind` resolves to the base member.

snippet.label: abstract method and sealed override
snippet.explanation: Line 3: `abstract` demands an override and forbids `new AuthHandler()`. Line 4: `virtual` provides a default that derived types may replace. Line 10: `sealed override` closes the `IsExpired` slot — no child of `LtiHandler` can override it (and none can exist because `LtiHandler` is sealed).

snippet.label: Template Method with protected hooks
snippet.explanation: Line 3: public `Parse` is the Template Method — shared algorithm. Line 5: `Validate` is private — not overridable. Line 12: `ParseCore` is `protected abstract` — the variation point for derived types. This is a practical, small virtual surface.

snippet.label: Covariant return types (C# 9+)
snippet.explanation: Since C# 9, an override can return a type derived from the base return type. The method table slot still dispatches to LtiFactory.Create, but callers through HandlerFactory see Handler. Covariance applies to return types only — parameter types are not covariant on overrides.

blocks.title: Polymorphism across languages
rows: Just assign a method on the derived class or prototype
No language distinction — always replaces on prototype
Blocks further override at metadata level

blocks.title: Calling virtual methods from constructors
blocks.body: If a base constructor calls a virtual method, the derived override runs before derived field initializers finish. The override may read uninitialized state. Keep constructors free of virtual calls.

blocks.title: Using new by accident after a refactor
blocks.body: After renaming a base method, the compiler may accept `new` instead of `override` if the base method is not virtual. The code compiles but dispatch breaks silently. Always check whether the base member is virtual before choosing `new` vs `override`.

blocks.text: Virtual dispatch walks the object's method table (vtable) at run time: the call site loads the slot for the compile-time member, then the Common Language Runtime (CLR) resolves it against the actual type. The Just-In-Time (JIT) compiler can **devirtualize** when it proves the receiver type — sealed classes, sealed override, or a local variable of a concrete type may inline the target and skip the indirect call. Covariant returns (C# 9+) let an override return a more derived type without changing the vtable slot semantics. The constructor trap is real: if a base constructor calls a virtual method, the derived override runs before derived field initializers finish, so the override may read default(T) fields. How to prove it in production: BenchmarkDotNet comparing sealed versus unsealed hot paths, or a debugger breakpoint on the derived override fired from the base constructor stack frame.

blocks.title: Tradeoffs at senior level
rows: Compatibility contract; harder to change later
Dispatch through base type ignores derived member
Callers get narrower type without extra cast
Derived override sees uninitialized derived state

snippet.label: Constructor virtual call — the production bug
snippet.explanation: Base constructor runs before Derived field initializers. The override of Log executes with _tenant still at its default (null for a reference type). Strong teams keep base constructors free of virtual calls or use factory methods that call Init() after full construction.

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Saying "virtual and override are just like JavaScript prototype assignment" — C# has explicit slots, sealed override, and covariant returns. Claiming virtual calls are always slow — sealed types and devirtualization often eliminate the indirect call. Saying new and override are interchangeable — calling through the base type proves they are not. Strong answer: virtual opens a vtable slot; override replaces it; new hides; sealed enables devirtualization; never call virtual methods from base constructors.

interviewTakeaways: virtual/override is runtime vtable dispatch; new is compile-time hiding that does not replace the slot.
sealed override and sealed classes let the JIT devirtualize and inline hot paths.
Covariant returns (C# 9+) allow an override to return a more derived type than the base virtual method.

60s: Polymorphism is vtable dispatch. override replaces the slot; new hides. sealed enables devirtualization. Covariant returns since C# 9. Never call virtual methods from base constructors — derived override runs before derived fields initialize.
Follow-up: how would you prove devirtualization or measure virtual call cost on a hot auth handler path?
commonPitfalls: Saying new and override behave the same through a base reference — that answer gets rejected because dispatch proves otherwise.
Strong answer: override replaces the vtable slot; new creates a separate member visible only on the derived static type.
Calling virtual methods from base constructors — derived override runs before derived field initializers complete.
Assuming every virtual call pays full indirect cost — sealed types and JIT devirtualization often eliminate it.

jsTsCorrelations.note: JavaScript override is just assigning a function on the derived prototype. There is no virtual keyword; hiding versus override is not a language distinction.
TypeScript override is a compile-time check that a base method exists. It does not create a CLR slot. C# override is metadata enforced by the runtime.
